title: Evidence in Plain Sight
theme: Observation and evidence: noticing what is really there
objectives: I can explain how ten words describe noticing, missing, and how obvious a piece of evidence is.
I can use context clues to tell similar words apart, such as detect and discern, or evident and apparent.
I can place words on a line from hidden to obvious and defend my choices.
I can write about a clue using precise words instead of 'easy to see' or 'hard to see'.
rationale: Before sixth graders can support a claim they need words for what evidence is, how easy it is to notice, and how people miss it. The ten words split into acts of noticing (detect, discern, overlook), degrees of obviousness (subtle, evident, apparent, conspicuous, obscure) and the evidence itself (distinct, trace). Three words carry more than one sense (apparent, obscure, overlook) and one is a frequent confusable (distinct), so the unit trains students to check context before choosing a meaning. The words return in every inquiry, argument and cause-and-effect unit later in the year.

words.def: To find or notice something that is hidden or hard to see.
words.ex: Scientists use special cameras to detect heat that people cannot see.
words.ex2: The smoke alarm can detect even a faint trace of smoke in the hallway.
words.nonExample: A person who walks past a clue without seeing it has failed to detect it.

apps.academic: In science, instruments detect changes that our senses cannot.
apps.spoken: Can you detect a different smell in here?
apps.writing: Use detect when a character or a tool finds something that was hidden.

cloze.s: The doctor used a scan to ___ a tiny crack in the bone that no one had seen on the first X-ray.

cloze2.s: Bats use sound to ___ insects flying in total darkness.

misuse.s: I detected the surprise party because I walked past the house with my eyes closed and noticed nothing.
misuse.why: To detect means to find or notice something; noticing nothing is the opposite.

visual.alt: A magnifying glass beside a radar dish.

words.frame: A tool that can detect ___ is useful because ___.

words.def: To recognize or tell apart something that is not easy to see or understand.
words.ex: Through the fog, we could barely discern the outline of the lighthouse.
words.ex2: A good editor can discern which sentences carry the main idea and which can be cut.
words.nonExample: Reading a word printed in huge letters does not require discerning anything.

apps.academic: Readers discern a theme by noticing which ideas return again and again.
apps.spoken: I can't discern whether she is joking or serious.
apps.writing: Use discern when a character works to make sense of something unclear.

cloze.s: Through the thick fog, the sailors could barely ___ the dim shape of the dock ahead.

cloze2.s: It took Anika a while to ___ the real message hidden in his vague, rambling note.

misuse.s: The sign was enormous and bright, so we had to strain to discern it.
misuse.why: Discern is for things that are hard to see or understand; a huge bright sign needs no straining.

visual.alt: A sailboat barely visible in thick fog.

words.frame: I can discern the difference between ___ and ___ by ___.

words.def: So small or gentle that it is hard to notice, but still meaningful.
words.ex: The painter used subtle shades of gray, so the two walls looked almost the same.
words.ex2: Her subtle smile told me she already knew the secret.
words.nonExample: A flashing neon sign is not subtle.

apps.academic: Authors often show a character's feelings through subtle details instead of stating them.
apps.spoken: There's a subtle difference between the two flavors.
apps.writing: Use subtle for hints, shades, or changes that a reader must look closely to see.

cloze.s: The twins looked alike, but a ___ difference in the shape of their eyebrows let me tell them apart.

cloze2.s: Because the drop in temperature was so ___, the plants wilted before anyone realized the room was cooling.

misuse.s: The firefighter's siren was so subtle that it startled the whole neighborhood awake.
misuse.why: Subtle means hard to notice; a siren that wakes a whole neighborhood is loud and obvious.

visual.alt: A line from 'obvious' to 'hard to notice', with subtle near the hard-to-notice end.

words.frame: A subtle sign that someone is ___ is ___.

words.def: Easy to see or understand because the proof is clear.
words.ex: It was evident from the muddy boots by the door that someone had come in through the garden.
words.ex2: Pride was evident on his face as he held up the finished model.
words.nonExample: If the clues point in three different directions, the answer is not yet evident.

apps.academic: A writer makes a claim evident by pointing to the facts that support it.
apps.spoken: It's evident that you worked hard on this.
apps.writing: Use evident when clues make something clear without anyone having to say it.

cloze.s: With a trail of crumbs leading straight to the pantry, it was ___ who had eaten the cookies.

cloze2.s: The team's joy was ___ in every shout and hug after the final whistle.

misuse.s: It was evident that nobody could tell what had happened, since every clue was missing.
misuse.why: Evident means clear to see; if every clue is missing, nothing is evident.

visual.alt: A glowing lightbulb beside a pair of eyes.

words.def: Plain to see; clear to anyone who looks.

senses.def: Seeming to be true, though it may not be.
senses.example: The apparent winner of the race was later found to have cut across the field.

words.ex: The tired look on the runner's face made her exhaustion apparent to everyone.
words.ex2: For no apparent reason, the lights flickered twice and then stayed on.
words.nonExample: A secret that no one has found yet is not apparent.

apps.academic: Historians separate the apparent cause of a war from its deeper causes.
apps.spoken: The problem became apparent when the app crashed.
apps.writing: Use apparent for what is plain to see, and watch for the second meaning, what only seems true.

cloze.s: Dark clouds and a rising wind made it ___ that the picnic would soon end.

cloze2.s: The ___ trouble with the plan was that it needed three people and we had only two.

misuse.s: It was apparent that no one could see the problem, since it was hidden behind a locked door.
misuse.why: Apparent means plain to see; something hidden behind a locked door is not apparent.

visual.alt: A person looking up at dark clouds gathering.

words.def: Easy to notice because it stands out from what is around it.
words.ex: The bright orange cone was conspicuous in the middle of the gray parking lot.
words.ex2: Dani felt conspicuous in a costume when everyone else at the party wore ordinary clothes.
words.nonExample: A gray moth resting on gray bark is not conspicuous.

apps.academic: Some animals have conspicuous colors that warn other animals to stay away.
apps.spoken: I felt conspicuous standing alone by the door.
apps.writing: Use conspicuous for something that draws the eye, sometimes in an uncomfortable way.

cloze.s: The giant red hat made the speaker ___ in a crowd of people wearing dark coats.

cloze2.s: Hunters wear bright orange vests to make themselves ___ in the green woods.

misuse.s: The spy chose a conspicuous disguise: a plain gray coat that blended into the crowd.
misuse.why: Conspicuous means standing out; a plain coat that blends in is the opposite.

visual.alt: A person in a bright vest standing out against green trees.

words.def: Hard to see or understand because it is unclear or little known.

senses.def: To hide something or make it hard to see.
senses.example: Thick clouds obscure the mountaintop for most of the winter.

words.ex: The obscure poem was so rarely read that even the librarian had never heard of it.
words.ex2: The meaning of the old map's symbols stayed obscure until we found the key.
words.nonExample: A famous song heard on the radio every day is not obscure.

apps.academic: An obscure source may be hard to check because few people have used it.
apps.spoken: The directions were so obscure that we got lost.
apps.writing: Use obscure for meanings that are hard to find or facts that few people know.

cloze.s: The instructions were so ___ that nobody in the class could tell what the first step was.

cloze2.s: Few people had heard of the ___ band, which played only in one small town.

misuse.s: Everyone knew the obscure singer, whose songs played on every radio station each day.
misuse.why: Obscure means little known; a singer on every radio station is well known.

visual.alt: An old scroll half hidden in mist.

words.frame: An obscure fact is one that ___.

words.def: To miss seeing something, or to ignore it by mistake.

senses.def: To have a view of a place from a higher spot.
senses.example: Our hotel room overlooks the harbor.

words.ex: Maya overlooked the typo in her title because she had read it so many times.
words.ex2: Detectives are trained not to overlook anything, even a button on the floor.
words.nonExample: A student who reads every line of the directions twice has not overlooked anything.

apps.academic: When you proofread, you can overlook your own mistakes because you know what you meant to write.
apps.spoken: Sorry, I overlooked that part of your email.
apps.writing: Use overlook for a detail someone misses, and for a view when a place looks out over something.

cloze.s: I read the test twice, but I still ___ the last question printed on the back page.

cloze2.s: Don't ___ the small print; it explains the rules that matter most.

misuse.s: The inspector overlooked the crack because she studied every inch of the wall with a flashlight.
misuse.why: To overlook is to miss something; an inspector who studies every inch would not miss it.

visual.alt: A student covering their eyes beside a page with a small mistake.

words.def: Clearly different from others; separate and easy to tell apart.

senses.example: There was a distinct smell of smoke in the hallway.

words.ex: Each bird in the marsh has its own distinct call, so experts can tell them apart with their eyes closed.
words.ex2: The two ideas sound alike, but they are distinct and belong in separate paragraphs.
words.nonExample: Two shades of blue that look exactly the same are not distinct.

apps.academic: Good paragraphs each have a distinct main idea.
apps.spoken: My two cats have distinct personalities.
apps.writing: Use distinct when you want to stress that things are separate and easy to tell apart.

cloze.s: The twins have ___ personalities: one loves crowds and the other prefers a quiet corner.

cloze2.s: The map shows four ___ regions, each in its own color, with a clear line between them.

misuse.s: The two songs were so distinct that no one could tell which was which.
misuse.why: Distinct things are easy to tell apart; if no one can tell them apart, they are not distinct.

visual.alt: A blue circle and a red square set clearly apart.

words.def: A small sign, mark, or amount left behind that shows something was there.

senses.def: To follow or find the origin of something step by step.
senses.example: The librarian traced the quotation back to an old book of poems.

words.ex: The detective found no trace of the thief, not even a footprint.
words.ex2: A trace of cinnamon in the soup gave it a warm taste.
words.nonExample: A wide, well-marked trail is not a trace.

apps.academic: Scientists look for traces of water on other planets.
apps.spoken: There wasn't a trace of snow by noon.
apps.writing: Use trace for a tiny remaining sign, such as a trace of smoke or a trace of fear.

cloze.s: After the flood, there was not a ___ of the little wooden bridge; the river had carried it all away.

cloze2.s: The chemist found a ___ of copper in the water, far too small to see.

misuse.s: A trace of paint covered the whole fence in thick, glossy coats.
misuse.why: A trace is a tiny amount; thick coats that cover a fence are not a trace.

visual.alt: Faint paw prints fading in a patch of snow.

words.frame: I could find no trace of ___ except ___.

passage.title: The Missing Blue Notebook
paras: On Monday morning, Ines found the science room in a small uproar. The class field notebook, which held three weeks of weather measurements, was missing from its shelf. Ms. Tran asked everyone to look carefully. "Do not overlook anything," she said, "even something that seems small."

At first nothing about the room seemed unusual. Then Ines knelt beside the shelf and noticed a thin line in the chalk dust, a subtle mark that most people would have stepped right past. Beside it she found a trace of blue ink, no bigger than a freckle. "Something was dragged across here," she told Omar.

Omar pointed at the open window. "It's apparent what happened," he said. "A gust of wind blew the notebook off the shelf and out of the room." But Ines could detect a flaw in that idea. The window was on the other side of the room, and the dust beneath it was smooth. "It is evident that the notebook did not leave that way," she said. "A breeze strong enough to move it would have left a mark."

She followed the faint ink line to the supply closet. The door stood open a crack, and inside, the shelves were packed with boxes, tape, and jars of colored pencils. In the dim light Ines could barely discern a blue corner at the back, half hidden behind a stack of obscure old textbooks that most students had never even opened.

Ms. Tran studied the bent cover and smiled. "The custodian moved the supply cart on Friday," she said. "The notebook must have slid onto it." Ines had seen two distinct sets of marks in the dust: a long drag mark from the notebook and the narrow tracks of cart wheels. Together they told the whole story. "Your sharp eyes saved three weeks of data," Ms. Tran said. Ines grinned. A bright blue notebook is usually conspicuous, she thought, but even the most conspicuous object can vanish when it ends up in the wrong place.

qs.q: In paragraph 2, the word "subtle" most nearly means
qs.why: The line in the dust is something most people would have stepped past, so it is hard to notice.

qs.q: Why does Ines doubt Omar's idea that the wind blew the notebook away?
choices: She was told the window had been locked all weekend.
She does not like Omar's ideas.
The window was far from the shelf and the dust under it was smooth.
She saw the notebook lying outside.
qs.why: Ines reasons that a breeze strong enough to move the notebook would have disturbed the dust under the window, and it did not.

qs.q: Which detail best supports Ines's claim that something was dragged across the shelf?
choices: A thin line in the chalk dust and a trace of blue ink
The open window on the far side of the room
The jars of colored pencils in the closet
Ms. Tran's smile at the end
qs.why: The line in the dust and the ink are marks left on the shelf itself, so they show the notebook moving across it.

qs.q: In paragraph 4, the phrase "obscure old textbooks" suggests that the books were
qs.why: The text says most students had never even opened them, which shows they were little known and rarely used.

qs.q: Which statement best expresses a central idea of the passage?
choices: Wind is the most common cause of lost objects.
Noticing small clues and testing explanations can solve a problem.
Custodians should not move supplies on Fridays.
Notebooks should always be kept in closets.
qs.why: Ines solves the puzzle by noticing marks in the dust and by checking Omar's idea against what she sees.

constructed.prompt: Describe two clues in a mystery, one subtle and one conspicuous. Use both words and say what each clue shows.
look: gives a concrete clue for each
shows the contrast in how easy each is to notice
constructed.model: In my mystery, the conspicuous clue is a bright red glove lying in the middle of the hallway. The subtle clue is a tiny scratch on the lock, which shows that someone opened it without a key.

makes clear what the mark is or might be

teacher.overview: Students learn ten words for noticing, missing, and judging how obvious evidence is, read a short mystery, place words on a hidden-to-obvious line, and practice choosing the right sense of words with more than one meaning.

notes.va.detect.v: Detect is about finding that something exists, often with a tool or trained attention. Contrast it with discern, which is about telling parts apart once you are looking. Have students sort things people detect with instruments from things they detect with their senses.
notes.va.discern.v: Discern goes one step past detect: you already see something and work to make it out or tell it from something else. Students often use it as a fancy synonym for see; push them to name what was hard to make out.
notes.va.subtle.adj: The b is silent, which makes spelling hard; teach the pronunciation first. Subtle does not mean weak: a subtle hint can change how a reader understands a whole scene. Ask students to find a subtle detail in a picture and say what it suggests.
notes.va.evident.adj: Evident is tied to proof: something is evident because the evidence shows it. Connect it to its family word evidence and ask students to name the evidence that makes a conclusion evident. Likely confusion with apparent; treat them as close synonyms and save the difference for apparent.
notes.va.apparent.adj: Apparent has two senses: plain to see, and seeming true but possibly not (the apparent winner). Context decides, so have students read the sentence before and after. Teach the phrase 'for no apparent reason' as a chunk.
notes.va.conspicuous.adj: Conspicuous is about contrast with the background, not about size. Use camouflage as a counter-example. Notice that it can feel negative when a person is the thing that stands out.
notes.va.obscure.adj: Obscure as an adjective has two close meanings (unclear; little known) and a verb sense (to hide). Students see the verb in weather and text; point to the stress change in pronunciation only if asked. Have them sort sentences by sense.
notes.va.overlook.v: Overlook is the opposite action to detect. Its second sense (a view) is common in real estate and travel writing; show a photo of a house overlooking a lake. Models of proofreading make the first sense concrete: we overlook what we expect to see.
notes.va.distinct.adj: Often confused with distinctive (marking something as special). Distinct means separate or clear; keep distinctive for a later conversation. The second sense (a distinct smell) comes from the same idea of standing apart from background noise.
notes.va.trace.n: Trace is a noun for what is left (a trace of smoke) and a verb for following something back to its source; the unit teaches the noun and uses the verb as a second sense. Students may think a trace must be visible; a trace of salt can be tasted, not seen.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'Ines sees a thin line in the dust. Most people would walk past it, so it is hard to notice. That is what subtle means. Later she can barely make out a blue corner in dim light, which is why the author says discern, not just see. I can prove each word with a detail from the text.'
discuss: Which would you rather be as an investigator, someone who detects small things or someone who explains big things? Why?
What is the difference between something that is hard to notice and something that is hard to understand?
misconceptions: Obscure and obvious are close in meaning because they look alike.
Overlook only means to ignore on purpose.
Distinct and distinctive mean exactly the same thing.
extend: Photograph or sketch a scene with one subtle detail and one conspicuous detail, then write captions using both words.
Rewrite the passage as a news report in which the reporter uses at least four words from the unit.
teacher.reviewAdvice: Revisit the three ways of judging a claim from unit 1 (perceptive, skeptical, candid) alongside evident and apparent two days later, and again at one week. Ask which of those character words would help someone detect, and which would help someone overlook.

frames: I could detect ___, but I could only barely discern ___.
The clue was subtle because ___, but ___ was conspicuous.
It is evident that ___, so I would not overlook ___.
wida.oral: Partner A describes a clue without using the word. Partner B decides whether it is subtle, evident, or conspicuous and says why.

needsReview: Spanish glosses not reviewed by a native speaker: poco claro (obscure; oscuro also exists but means dark first), pasar por alto, llamativo, rastro, discernir.

apparent: Spanish gloss 'evidente' fits the 'plain to see' sense; 'aparente' is a cognate that usually matches the 'seeming' sense (a false-friend risk), so cognate is marked false for the taught sense.
Sense boundary: obscure (adj) and its verb sense; overlook 'view' sense; distinct 'clear' second sense. Confirm these second senses are age-appropriate to teach together.

Fact claims in word records: bats use sound to detect insects; scientists use special cameras to detect heat; some animals have conspicuous warning colors; hunters wear bright orange vests. All are standard and believed true.
Passage is fiction; no factual claims.
